section.title: Sing to the Lord a New Song
section.sectionRationale: An enthronement hymn whose lines were sung by David when the ark entered Jerusalem, this psalm summons all the earth, not Israel alone, to sing a new song to the reigning LORD and to await His coming to judge the world in righteousness, a hope fulfilled in Christ's global reign and return.
section.thesis: The LORD who made the heavens, unlike the worthless idols of the nations, deserves a new song from all the earth, and every family of peoples is summoned to worship Him because He is coming to judge the world in righteousness and truth.
section.frameNote: Three movements: a threefold call to sing a new song and declare God's glory among the nations, verses 1-6; a summons for the families of the peoples to ascribe Him glory and worship in holiness, verses 7-9; and creation's joy at the LORD's coming reign of righteous judgment, verses 10-13.

units.label: Sing to the Lord, all the earth
units.note: a call to declare His glory among the nations

verses.text: Sing to the LORD a {{chadash|new}} song; sing to the LORD, all the earth.
Sing to the LORD, bless His name; proclaim His salvation day after day.
Declare His {{kavod|glory}} among the nations, His wonders among all peoples.
For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; He is to be feared above all gods.
For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens.
Splendor and majesty are before Him; strength and beauty fill His sanctuary.

units.label: Ascribe to the Lord glory and strength
units.note: a summons to the families of the peoples

verses.text: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the nations, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.
Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name; bring an offering and enter His courts.
Worship the LORD in the splendor of His holiness; tremble before Him, all the earth.

units.label: He is coming to judge the earth
units.note: creation's joy at the LORD's righteous reign

verses.text: Declare among the nations: "The LORD {{malak|reigns}}!" The world is firmly established; it cannot be moved; He will judge the peoples with equity.
Let the heavens be glad and the earth rejoice; let the sea resound, and all that fills it.
Let the fields exult, and all that is in them. Then all the trees of the forest will sing for joy
before the LORD, for He is coming, He is coming to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness.

chadash.gloss: New, fresh. A new song is called for whenever God acts in fresh salvation; Revelation 5:9 pictures the redeemed singing just such a new song to the Lamb who was slain.

kavod.gloss: Glory, weight, or honor. God's kavod, His weighty splendor, is to be declared among every nation, not confined to Israel; the New Testament shows this glory now radiating from Christ, John 1:14.

malak.gloss: To reign, be king. The declaration 'the LORD reigns' anchors this whole cluster of psalms; Revelation 11:15 answers it directly, 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.'

basic.context: This psalm, whose language David used when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, calls not just Israel but all the earth and every family of nations to sing a new song to the LORD. Unlike the powerless idols of the nations, He alone made the heavens, and He is coming to judge the world with perfect righteousness.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's global scope, 'all the earth,' 'the nations,' 'all peoples,' is not merely poetic exaggeration but a genuine missionary summons rooted in the promise to Abraham that all families of the earth would be blessed, fulfilled at last in the gospel going to every nation.
basic.originalLanguages: The call is for a chadash, new, song, sung whenever God acts in fresh salvation. His kavod, glory, is to be declared among the nations, not hoarded by Israel alone. And the announcement that the LORD malak, reigns, anchors the whole psalm's confidence in His coming righteous judgment.
basic.typology: The 'new song' anticipates the new song of the redeemed before the Lamb's throne, Revelation 5:9; the summons for 'all peoples' to worship anticipates the ingathering of every nation into Christ's kingdom; and the LORD's coming to judge the earth anticipates Christ's return as Judge.
basic.christ: Romans 15:9-12 gathers texts like this psalm to show that Christ came so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy; the declaration 'the LORD reigns' finds its fulfillment when 'the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' Revelation 11:15, and His coming to judge the world anticipates Christ's return as the righteous Judge, Acts 17:31.
basic.god: God is Creator of the heavens, unlike the powerless idols of the nations, worthy of glory and strength from every family of peoples, and the coming Judge whose righteous rule will finally set creation itself singing in joy rather than groaning under the curse.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 15:9-12 quotes psalms like this one to show Christ came to bring the Gentiles to glorify God. Revelation 5:9 pictures the redeemed from every nation singing a new song to the Lamb. Revelation 11:15 answers this psalm's cry that 'the LORD reigns.' Acts 17:31 shows God has fixed a day to judge the world through the Man He has appointed.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's summons for all the earth and every family of nations to sing a new song to the reigning LORD runs forward to the day when people from every tribe and tongue gather around the Lamb's throne, and to Christ's certain return to judge the world in perfect righteousness.

context.literary:
Psalm 96 is built on repetition, and the repetition does the arguing. The verb 'sing' opens the psalm three times in verses 1 and 2, and 'ascribe' opens three lines in verses 7 and 8. The name of the LORD is named again and again, so that the nations are not allowed to praise anything else. The psalm has three movements. Verses 1 to 6 are a call to sing and to tell the nations, with a reason in verses 4 to 6. Verses 7 to 9 turn to the nations themselves, now addressed directly as 'families of the nations' and told what to do. Verses 10 to 13 widen again, to the cosmos: heavens, earth, sea, fields and forest, all called to joy because the LORD is coming.

The movement is outward in rings. It begins with 'Sing to the LORD,' a call that could be spoken in the congregation, reaches 'among the nations' in verse 3, reaches 'families of the nations' in verse 7, and ends with every tree of the forest. A second pattern runs inward: verses 1 to 3 say what to do among the nations, verses 4 to 6 say why, verses 7 to 9 tell the nations to come into His courts, and verse 13 brings the Judge Himself to the earth. The psalm starts in Israel's mouth and ends with the trees singing to the LORD, and everything in between is a widening circle.

The climax is the doubled 'He is coming' of verse 13. The psalm has been moving toward an arrival, and the structure teaches that joy comes before the event. Creation rejoices because the Judge approaches, not because He has finished. Verse 10's 'The LORD reigns' is the declaration, and verses 11 to 13 are the response to it.
context.historical:
The psalm has no title in the Hebrew, but its words appear in the Book of Chronicles in the hymn David gave to Asaph and his brothers when the ark was brought into Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 16:23-33. The Chronicler's hymn is a composite, with the first part matching Psalm 105 and the last matching Psalm 106, and in the middle lies the substance of Psalm 96. Whether David wrote it or a later poet drew from the same stock, the setting it assumes is a celebration around the presence of God: an offering, a sanctuary, courts to enter, a procession.

Israel's neighbours had their own songs to their gods, and the psalm knows it. Verse 5 says 'all the gods of the nations are idols,' and in the ancient world that was a daring sentence, since every city had its patron deity and every victory was credited to one. Israel, small and surrounded, was claiming that none of them was real and that the God who made the heavens was the God of the whole earth. The psalm is sung in a world where the nations are not yet listening, and it speaks to them as if they will.

The invitation to 'bring an offering and enter His courts' in verse 8 would have meant something concrete to Israel: a real gift carried up to a real altar. Gentiles were not barred from every approach to Israel's God, since foreigners could bring offerings, but the courts were Israel's. The psalm pictures a day when the nations themselves arrive with gifts. Isaiah draws the same picture, where 'all nations will stream' to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 2:2, and the prophet says the peoples will say 'He will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths,' Isaiah 2:3.
context.canonical:
Psalm 96 is one of a cluster of kingship psalms that runs from 93 to 99, and its closest sibling is Psalm 98. Both begin 'Sing to the LORD a new song' and both end with the LORD coming 'to judge the earth,' in nearly the same words, Psalm 98:9. Between them they set the standard for the church's hymnbook. The refrain 'the LORD reigns' recurs in Psalms 93, 97 and 99 as well. The new song also appears in Psalm 33:3, 40:3, 144:9 and 149:1, and in Isaiah 42:10, where it is sung from the ends of the earth.

The psalm is taken up in Chronicles, where it is placed in David's mouth at the ark's arrival. The prophets echo its mission, especially Isaiah 40:9 and 52:7, where the herald says to Zion 'Your God reigns,' and where the Hebrew verb for 'proclaim' is the one from which the Greek word for gospel grew. In the New Testament the nations' worship is the theme of Paul's argument in Romans 15:9-12, where he gathers Psalms and Isaiah to show that the Gentiles were always meant to glorify God for His mercy.

The ending of the psalm is taken up by the final book of the Bible. In Revelation the new song is sung before the Lamb, Revelation 5:9 and 14:3. The declaration of Psalm 96:10 finds its echo in Revelation 11:15, 'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ,' and the angel with the eternal gospel calls people to 'Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth,' Revelation 14:6-7, in words that could have been lifted from verses 4 and 5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted Israel to understand that worship was never meant to be kept in the family. The God who delivered them was the God who made the heavens, and a God that size has a claim on every people. The psalm tells Israel to do something with that knowledge: declare it, among the nations, day after day. Praise is turned outward, toward people who do not yet know the name.

He also meant to give Israel courage. A small nation in a world of powerful gods could easily feel its faith was a private eccentricity. Verses 4 and 5 answer that with a flat sentence: the nations' gods are nothing, and the LORD made everything. The argument for going out to the nations is also a support for staying faithful at home.

The final movement is an invitation to hope. The LORD is coming, and He is coming to put things right, to judge with equity, in righteousness, in faithfulness. The psalm does not dread that arrival; it sings because of it. The psalmist wanted his hearers to see judgment as good news for the world, a day when the crooked are made straight and the trees may laugh. That was a bold thing to say to a people who had known wars and exile, and it was meant to shape how they lived between the promise and the day.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a hymn, so most of its verbs are commands, but they are commands of worship and witness, not of conquest. 'Declare His glory among the nations' is a duty to speak, not an instruction to impose. The invitation to 'bring an offering and enter His courts' describes a temple that stood for Israel's worship, and Christians do not read it as a requirement to build one. The New Testament says the place where the nations meet God is now a person, John 2:19-21 and Hebrews 10:19-20, so the gift is now the gift of a life and of praise, Hebrews 13:15.

What carries over is the direction of the psalm. The church inherited the commission to make the LORD's glory known among all peoples, Matthew 28:19-20, and the new song is still the church's song, Revelation 5:9. Careful readers should also notice what the psalm does not say. It does not say that all nations are already saved, nor that the LORD's judgment is a threat to the faithful. It describes a summons and a coming, and the proper response to both is praise now and witness now. The psalm teaches us to sing before we see everything, because the LORD reigns already.

debates.question: Does verse 13, 'He is coming to judge the earth,' point to a past historical act, or forward to a final, still-future judgment?

views.label: The verse chiefly celebrates a past or repeated act of God's righteous rule over history
views.case: In its original setting, the psalm may reflect God's ongoing governance and vindication of His people within history, not only a single final event.

views.label: The verse points forward to God's final, universal judgment of all the earth
views.case: The scope, 'the world,' 'the peoples,' 'in righteousness,' exceeds any single historical event, and the New Testament treats this coming judgment as still future, fixed to a day, Acts 17:31.

debates.bearing: Both readings cohere: the God who has always ruled and vindicated His people in history is the same God who will bring final, universal judgment through Christ.

debates.question: What is the relationship between Psalm 96 and 1 Chronicles 16:23-33?

views.label: David composed the hymn, and Psalm 96 and Chronicles both preserve it
views.case: Chronicles presents the words as David's hymn for the ark's arrival, 1 Chronicles 16:7, and the psalm's themes of offering, courts and sanctuary fit a celebration of God's presence at the ark. The psalter and the Chronicler may each have drawn on a single Davidic original.

views.label: A later poet composed the psalm, and the Chronicler quoted it
views.case: The Chronicler builds his hymn from pieces of Psalms 105, 96 and 106, which look like completed psalms in their own right. On this view the psalm already existed as part of a collection and the Chronicler assembled it for David's scene.

views.label: The two texts show a hymn being adapted for new occasions
views.case: The small differences, such as 'strength and beauty fill His sanctuary' in Psalm 96:6 against 'strength and joy fill His dwelling' in 1 Chronicles 16:27, suggest a living liturgy reworded as it was used, and not a single fixed text.

debates.bearing: The question of authorship does not change what the psalm teaches. Either way the words were sung at the center of Israel's worship, and the Chronicler, writing for a rebuilt community, treated them as a hymn that still spoke to his own day.

study.originalLanguages:
The command of verse 1, 'Sing to the LORD a new song,' uses the verb shir, to sing, three times in verses 1 and 2, in the form of an imperative addressed to the whole earth. The 'new song' is shir chadash, and the phrase recurs across the Psalter and in Isaiah 42:10. What makes a song new is not its tune but its occasion: each time God acts in fresh salvation, the old songs are not enough. The psalm makes the point by giving the new song a global audience, 'all the earth.'

In verse 2 the verb 'proclaim' is basser, from the root that means to announce good news, and it is used of a messenger carrying news of victory. The Greek Old Testament renders it with a verb that means to bring the gospel. Isaiah uses it for the herald of Zion in Isaiah 40:9 and 52:7, and the New Testament word for gospel grew from the same ground. The thing proclaimed is God's 'salvation,' yeshuah, a word related to the name Jesus.

Verse 5 makes a pun. The nations' gods are elilim, a word that sounds like elohim, 'gods,' but means 'worthless things' or 'nothings.' The psalm takes the ordinary word for gods and replaces it with a word that means almost nothing. Against that stands the verb of making: 'it is the LORD who made the heavens.' The contrast is between beings that are named and a Being who makes.

The verb 'ascribe' in verses 7 and 8 is havu, from the word 'to give.' It is the same verb Psalm 29:1-2 uses, where the heavenly beings are told to ascribe glory to the LORD. In Psalm 96 the audience has changed. In Psalm 29 it is the members of the divine court; here it is 'families of the nations,' mishpechot, the word for clans. The whole human family is invited to do what the angels do. Glory is something we give back, not something we invent. The object, 'the glory due His name,' says that there is a measure, and the nations have been underpaying.

Verse 9 says 'tremble before Him,' from chul, a verb for writhing or shaking, as in labour pains, joined to 'the splendor of His holiness.' Worship here is not casual; the body shakes. In verse 6 the pairing 'splendor and majesty,' hod and hadar, are royal attributes, and 'strength and beauty' in the sanctuary connect His kingship to the place of worship.

The announcement 'The LORD reigns' in verse 10 is malak YHWH, used in psalms 93, 97 and 99, and the verb can also be heard as 'has become king,' an enthronement cry. The final 'He is coming' in verse 13 uses a participle, ba, which means 'is coming' and suggests the arrival is under way. The 'equity' of verse 10 is meisharim, straightness, and the 'faithfulness' of verse 13 is emunah, which is the firmness of a thing that does not fail. Together these describe a judge who sets crooked things straight and does not go back on His word.

typology.fulfillment: Each time God saved Israel, a new song followed, as at the sea, Exodus 15:1, and in the psalms. The pattern escalates in the book of Revelation, where a new song is sung before the Lamb: 'Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9. The song Israel sang for a deliverance in history is now sung for a deliverance that costs a life and reaches every people. The type falls short because earlier songs celebrated temporary rescues, while the final song celebrates a salvation that cannot be undone.

typology.type: Declaring His glory among the nations, verses 2 and 3
typology.fulfillment: Israel's calling was to be a light to the nations, but the psalm's command to declare the glory among the peoples was mostly unmet. Simeon calls the infant Jesus 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel,' Luke 2:32. Paul and Barnabas applied the word from Isaiah, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth,' Acts 13:47, to the apostolic mission. The Great Commission is the psalm's imperative widened: 'go and make disciples of all nations,' Matthew 28:19. The type is limited because Israel's declaration depended on a temple and a people, while the church's depends on the risen Christ who is with them always.

typology.type: The LORD coming to judge the earth, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: The psalm celebrates the arrival of God as Judge, and the New Testament says that the arrival is tied to the return of Jesus. 'When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne,' Matthew 25:31, and Paul says that God will judge the world 'by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31. The correspondence is exact at the level of the coming Judge and the righteous standard. The escalation is that the Judge is also the Savior who died for the world. The type falls short only in that the psalm does not name the person through whom it will happen.

typology.type: Creation rejoicing before the coming King, verses 11 and 12
typology.fulfillment: The heavens, earth, sea, fields and forest are called to rejoice, and Paul gives the reason in Romans 8:19-21, where the creation 'waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God' and will be set free from bondage to decay. The psalm's joy is the joy of creation anticipating liberation. The pattern is fulfilled in the new heaven and new earth of Revelation 21:1-4, where the former things have passed away. The type is partial because the psalm pictures only rejoicing, while the New Testament explains that the creation is also groaning now, waiting for what has been promised.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through its welcome to the nations. Paul collects several psalms in Romans 15:9-12 and says that Christ became a servant 'so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.' The command of Psalm 96 to sing among the nations is part of the evidence he gathers, and he ends with Isaiah's promise that 'The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.' The psalm's global scope is not a distant ideal. It describes what Christ came to do.

It leads to Christ in its declaration of kingship. 'The LORD reigns' is what the psalm tells the nations to say, and the New Testament says the reign has been given to Jesus, who said 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me,' Matthew 28:18, and whom God 'exalted to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9. Revelation brings the declaration to its climax: 'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever,' Revelation 11:15. Christ does not replace the LORD of the psalm; He is the LORD's reign arriving in person.

It leads to Christ in the content of the new song. The song of Revelation 5:9 praises the Lamb because He was slain. The psalm asks for a new song because of God's salvation, and the New Testament says what that salvation cost. The song Israel sang was always one the nations would join, and Revelation shows them joining it. The angel with the eternal gospel calls people to worship 'the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea,' Revelation 14:7, which is verse 5 addressed to the world.

It leads to Christ in the coming Judge. The psalm says the LORD will judge 'in righteousness' and 'in His faithfulness,' and Paul tells Athens that God will judge the world 'with justice by the Man He has appointed,' and gave proof 'by raising Him from the dead,' Acts 17:31. Jesus Himself says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22. That tells us why the judgment of verse 13 is good news: the Judge is the one who died for sinners and rose. Believers can sing because they know who is coming.

A caution: the psalm never names a coming Messiah, and the 'He' of verse 13 is the LORD. The Christian reading comes from the New Testament's identification of the returning Lord Jesus with the coming LORD of the psalm, and does not treat the creatures and trees as coded pictures of the church.
study.god:
The psalm presents a God whose claim is universal. He is to be praised by 'all the earth,' feared 'above all gods,' and declared to all peoples. There is no local deity here, no god of a hill or a tribe. The reason given is that He made the heavens. The claim to the nations is based on ownership and authorship: what He made He has the right to be praised by. The logic is the opposite of imperialism, because the God who claims the world is the one who gave it.

He is utterly distinct from the idols. The psalm does not argue against them at length. It says they are nothings and moves on. Elsewhere Scripture mocks them as gods with mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see, Psalm 135:15-18, and as things that must be carried, Isaiah 46:7. The LORD, by contrast, made what they are fashioned from. Verse 6 adds that splendor and majesty are before Him, strength and beauty in His sanctuary, so His glory is not a burden but something that draws.

He is to be feared and He is to be enjoyed. The command to 'tremble before Him' in verse 9 stands next to the joy of verses 11 and 12. The God of the psalm is not a dilemma between awe and delight. The reverence is the ground on which the joy stands, which is why the creation can rejoice even as it awaits the Judge.

He is a King who judges. 'He will judge the peoples with equity' and 'the world in righteousness and the peoples in His faithfulness.' The psalm holds together a world that is 'firmly established' and a world in need of judgment. The stability is the stability of a righteous throne, and the judgment is the work of a king who cares that right is done. Faithfulness is among the qualities of the Judge, so His verdict can be trusted.

He is coming. The God of this psalm does not stay in His sanctuary. The repeated 'He is coming' describes a God who moves toward the earth. That matches the pattern of Scripture from the garden, where He walks, to the incarnation, where He comes in flesh, to the return, where He comes to judge and to dwell, Revelation 21:3.

For worship, the psalm asks for a church whose praise looks outward. A congregation that sings only for itself has not yet learned this hymn. It also teaches us to sing while the world still worships idols, because we know who made it, who reigns, and who is coming.

crossReferences.note: David's hymn at the arrival of the ark contains nearly the whole of Psalm 96. It shows the psalm at home in a festival of God's presence and gives it a king's voice. The small differences show the hymn being reshaped for use, and the setting ties its call to the nations to the place where God dwells.

The twin psalm, opening with the same 'new song' and ending with the same coming of the LORD to judge the earth 'with righteousness and the peoples with equity.' It adds the sea, the rivers and the mountains to the choir. Reading the two together shows how central the coming judgment was to Israel's hope.

The same command to 'ascribe to the LORD glory and strength' is given to the heavenly beings in Psalm 29 and to the families of the nations in Psalm 96. The two verses show the circle of worship widening from the heavenly court to the whole human family.

Isaiah commands a new song from the ends of the earth, from those who go down to the sea and from the islands. It takes the new song beyond Israel's borders to the coastlands, the far edges of the known world, in the same scope as Psalm 96's 'all the earth.'

The herald on the mountains proclaims peace and salvation and says to Zion 'Your God reigns!' It is the same announcement as Psalm 96:10 and uses the same root for proclaiming good news as verse 2, which is why the New Testament could call the message of Jesus a gospel.

The vision of all nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD to be taught His ways and to have their disputes judged. It puts the psalm's call for the nations to bring an offering and enter His courts into a prophetic picture of peace.

Paul strings together the Old Testament on the Gentiles' praise, including Psalm 117 and Isaiah, to show that Christ came so that the nations might glorify God for His mercy. It is the apostolic reading of psalms like this one, where the welcome to the nations is seen as always intended.

The new song is finally sung, before the Lamb, by people 'from every tribe and tongue and people and nation.' It is the psalm's summons fulfilled in the great gathering, and it tells us the cost, the Lamb's blood, that makes the nations' song possible.

When the seventh trumpet sounds, voices in heaven declare that 'The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ.' It is the fulfilment of the declaration 'The LORD reigns' that the psalm tells the nations to make, now attached to Christ.

An angel flies with the eternal gospel for every nation and says 'Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth.' The message is the psalm's summons condensed, with the coming judgment as the reason for worship.

Paul tells Athens that God has fixed a day to judge the world by a man He has appointed. It answers the question of who comes in verse 13 and makes the judgment a call to repent, much as the psalm makes it a reason for the nations to worship.

The creation waits eagerly to be set free and brought into the freedom of God's children. It supplies the reason that the heavens, sea and fields rejoice in verses 11 and 12: they will share in the liberation of the people of God, and their joy is the joy of a prisoner at the approach of release.

The previous psalm asks how long the wicked will 'exult,' using the verb that Psalm 96:12 gives to the fields. The exultation wrongly claimed by the wicked is finally given to creation as the Judge arrives, which is how the book answers the complaint.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers the question that opens the Bible: what is the world for? It was made to praise its Maker. Genesis 1 shows a creation in which the heavens, sea and land do what God says, and Job 38:7 pictures the morning stars singing as the earth is laid. Sin silenced the song, and idols replaced the Maker. Psalm 96 asks for the song to begin again, and begins it in Israel's voice.

It also recalls the call of Abraham, in which God promised that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. The psalm uses the word for families in verse 7 and calls them to ascribe glory to the LORD, which is the promised blessing pictured as worship. Israel's vocation as a kingdom of priests, with the nations as the audience for God's glory, is stated here more clearly than almost anywhere. The history of Israel shows how much of the vocation went unfulfilled, and the prophets kept restating it: the nations would come.

The story turns on Christ. The one in whom God's salvation appears is the light for the Gentiles and the glory of Israel, Luke 2:32, and He commissions His people to go to all nations, Matthew 28:19-20. The psalm's imperatives become a mission. The new song of verse 1 is given its reason in the cross, where the Lamb was slain and purchased people for God from every nation, Revelation 5:9. The church's missionary history is the psalm's command being obeyed.

The ending of the story is the ending of the psalm. The LORD comes, the nations worship, the creation rejoices. Revelation gathers a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' before the throne and the Lamb, Revelation 7:9-10, and shows a city whose gates are never shut, into which the nations bring their glory, Revelation 21:24-25. The sea that roared in the psalm is no more, and the trees of the forest, the fields and all that fill the earth join in the song. The world that was made to praise will at last do so. The Judge will arrive not as a threat to the creation but as its rescue, and the song that began as a command will become a description.

sermon.title: Declare His Glory Among the Nations
sermon.why: Preached directly from Psalm 96 and tagged by Desiring God as Scripture Psalm 96, Piper traces the psalm's own call to declare God's glory among the nations and summon them to sing, showing how this global vision is fulfilled in the church's mission and in Christ's coming kingdom.

quiz.q: Who is called to sing a new song to the LORD in verse 1?

options.text: All the earth, not Israel alone.
options.note: The psalm's opening summons is explicitly universal, 'sing to the LORD, all the earth.'

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The call goes far beyond the priesthood to all the earth.

options.text: Only the king and his royal court.
options.note: The psalm addresses all the earth, not a royal court alone.

options.text: Only the descendants of Abraham.
options.note: Israel is included, but the psalm's scope explicitly reaches beyond Israel to all the earth and every nation.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the gods of the nations in contrast to the LORD?

options.text: The gods of the nations are idols, but the LORD made the heavens.
options.note: Verse 5 draws a sharp contrast between powerless idols and the LORD who is Creator of the heavens.

options.text: The gods of the nations are lesser but still genuinely powerful rivals to the LORD.
options.note: The psalm calls them idols, worthless things, not genuine rival powers.

options.text: The gods of the nations share equally in creating the world with the LORD.
options.note: The psalm attributes creation of the heavens to the LORD alone.

options.text: The gods of the nations are simply different names for the same LORD.
options.note: The psalm treats them as idols, worthless, not as alternate names for the true God.

quiz.q: What are the families of the nations summoned to bring and do in verses 7-9?

options.text: Ascribe glory and strength to the LORD, bring an offering, and worship Him in the splendor of holiness.
options.note: These verses call the families of the nations to ascribe glory, bring an offering, enter His courts, and worship in holiness.

options.text: Bring their own idols to be blessed by the LORD.
options.note: The psalm calls the nations away from idols, not to bring idols for blessing.

options.text: Pay tribute exclusively to the king of Israel.
options.note: The summons is directed to the LORD Himself, not to Israel's human king.

options.text: Build a new temple for the LORD in their own lands.
options.note: The text calls for offerings and worship in His courts, not for building new temples elsewhere.

quiz.q: What declaration is to be made among the nations in verse 10?

options.text: "The LORD reigns!"
options.note: This central declaration anchors the psalm's confidence in God's stable, righteous rule over the whole world.

options.text: "The world will soon be destroyed."
options.note: The psalm declares the LORD's stable reign and coming righteous judgment, not the world's destruction.

options.text: "Israel alone will be spared judgment."
options.note: The declaration is about the LORD's universal reign, not about Israel's exemption from judgment.

options.text: "The nations must appoint their own judges."
options.note: The psalm assigns judgment to the LORD Himself, not to human judges appointed by the nations.

quiz.q: How does creation respond to the LORD's coming to judge the earth in verses 11-13?

options.text: The heavens, earth, sea, fields, and trees are pictured rejoicing and singing for joy.
options.note: The psalm personifies creation itself celebrating the LORD's coming righteous judgment.

options.text: Creation is pictured trembling in terror with no joy at all.
options.note: Trembling appears earlier at God's holiness, verse 9, but verses 11-13 emphasize gladness and joyful song.

options.text: Creation remains entirely silent and unmoved.
options.note: The text explicitly describes joyful, active response from creation, not silence.

options.text: Only the sea responds, while the land remains unaffected.
options.note: The heavens, earth, sea, fields, and trees are all named as responding, not the sea alone.

questions: The psalm calls for a 'new song,' fresh praise for fresh acts of God's salvation. What has God recently done in your life that deserves a genuinely new song of thanks, rather than routine praise?

This psalm insists that the idols of the nations are worthless while the LORD alone made the heavens. What modern 'idols,' wealth, status, control, quietly compete for the worship only God deserves in your life?
The families of the nations are summoned to worship 'in the splendor of His holiness.' What would it look like for your own worship to hold together both reverent awe and joyful gladness?
This psalm's global vision, 'declare His glory among the nations,' flows into the New Testament's call to make disciples of all nations. Where is God calling you to be part of that same declaration?

The psalm ends with creation itself rejoicing that the LORD is coming to judge the world in righteousness. How does hoping in Christ's certain, righteous return change how you respond to injustice you see today?

translationNotes.note: Much of this psalm's wording closely parallels the song David appointed to be sung when the ark of the covenant was brought into Jerusalem, recorded in 1 Chronicles 16:23-33.
The Hebrew word rendered 'idols' can carry the sense of 'worthless things' or 'nothings,' sharpening the contrast with the LORD who alone made the heavens.
The repetition 'He is coming, He is coming' in the Hebrew doubles for emphasis, underscoring the certainty of the LORD's coming judgment of the earth.
